Mozi, Volume 12

...they are unable to cause disaster or blessing. By insisting that there is no auspiciousness or inauspiciousness, the government becomes chaotic and the state endangered. Therefore, in the books of the former kings, it is also said: the character <term>Qi</term> <note>original: "亓", formerly written as "丌"</note> signifies arrogance. To emerge from such a state is inauspicious. This means that if one does evil, there is punishment; if one does good, there is reward. Master Mozi said to Gongmengzi, "Regarding the rites of mourning: for the ruler, parents, or wife, one wears mourning garments for three years. For uncles, brothers, and clansmen, one wears them for five months. For aunts, sisters, maternal uncles, and nephews, there are mourning periods of several months. Yet, in the intervals between mourning, you recite the three hundred <term>Odes</term> <gloss>Classic of Poetry</gloss>, play the three hundred <term>Odes</term> on stringed instruments, sing the three hundred <term>Odes</term>, and perform the dances of the three hundred <term>Odes</term>. If we follow your words, on what day would a gentleman listen to the affairs of government, and on what day would the common people attend to their work?" Gongmengzi said, "When the state is in chaos, one must bring order to it. Once it is ordered, then one practices rites and music. When the state is ordered, the people attend to their work. When the state is wealthy, then one practices rites and music." Master Mozi said, "If the order of the state <insert>Lu says five characters are missing here: 'is the reason for governing'</insert> is abandoned, then the order of the state is also lost. <summary>Master Mozi critiques the inconsistency of Gongmengzi's mourning practices and argues that prioritizing complex ritual and music over governance and practical labor leads to the decay of the state.</summary>
<keywords>Master Mozi, Gongmengzi, mourning rites, governance, ritual and music, state stability</keywords>
